title: Newtonian gravity
summary: An orbit is continuous free fall: gravitational acceleration curves the spacecraft velocity toward the primary.
details: Earth mu = 3.986004418 x 10^14 m^3/s^2. Circular speed is sqrt(mu/r). Radius is measured from Earth's center, not the surface. Our spherical Earth has radius 6,371 km.
regime: Weak gravitational fields and speeds small compared with c; spherical central body.
assumptions: Spherical Earth, negligible spacecraft mass, Newtonian two-body acceleration.
limitations: The implemented model is deliberately simplified; the cited reference describes a broader theory.
simulation_notes: Used by the current backend in the restricted form described in details.

title: Hohmann transfers
summary: Two tangential burns connect circular orbits through a transfer ellipse. The first changes the opposite apsis; the second circularizes.
details: The transfer semi-major axis is (r1+r2)/2. Vis-viva gives transfer speeds; subtract circular speeds for each burn. Earth orbital and lunar-distance transfers use exact elliptic Kepler sampling. The interplanetary model adds ideal planetary phase and patched-conic departure/capture budgets.
regime: Classical educational spacecraft simulation.
assumptions: Coplanar circular endpoints and instantaneous tangential burns in an Earth-only coast model.
limitations: The lunar-distance endpoint is not lunar interception, capture or landing; arbitrary endpoints need a different transfer model.
simulation_notes: Used by the current backend in the restricted form described in details.

title: The rocket equation
summary: Fuel demand grows exponentially with velocity change. Payload adds mass without adding propellant.
details: Isp is specific impulse in seconds; g0 = 9.80665 m/s^2. Wet mass includes dry mass, payload and fuel. A plan is infeasible if required delta-v exceeds the available budget. The ideal equation omits launch gravity and drag losses; those are integrated separately.
regime: Classical educational spacecraft simulation.
assumptions: Constant effective exhaust speed; positive Isp; wet, dry, payload and propellant masses are accounted for separately.
limitations: The implemented model is deliberately simplified; the cited reference describes a broader theory.
simulation_notes: Used by the current backend in the restricted form described in details.

title: PD flight control
equation: a_cmd = Kp(r_ref - r) + Kd(v_ref - v) + a_ref
summary: A fast deterministic controller follows a reference trajectory using position and velocity error, without making an LLM call at every timestep.
details: Docking uses Kp=0.08 s^-2 and Kd=0.6 s^-1 with reference acceleration and CW drift compensation. Commanded force is bounded at 500 N by default; attainable acceleration changes with spacecraft mass. A separate torque-limited attitude controller must match heading and angular rate. Both systems consume shared RCS propellant.
regime: Classical educational spacecraft simulation.
assumptions: Planar CW relative translation, exact state knowledge, prescribed rotating port, bounded force and a separate torque-limited planar attitude loop.
limitations: No general 6-DOF coupling, contact dynamics or navigation uncertainty. Relative orbital tides use the linear planar CW approximation. Runtime obstacles are geometric exclusion regions screened by candidate rollouts, not a general collision-avoidance guarantee.
simulation_notes: Implemented planar docking control with finite force/torque and fuel. No general 6-DOF control or contact mechanics.

title: Rotating docking ports
summary: A rotating station's port has a moving position and velocity. Reaching its position is insufficient: relative speed must also approach zero.
details: A port of radius R has position R[cos(omega*t),sin(omega*t)] in station LVLH coordinates, with velocity omega*R[-sin(omega*t),cos(omega*t)]. Docking checks position, relative speed, attitude angle and angular-rate error for a dwell interval. Station rpm is converted using omega=rpm*2*pi/60.

sources.title: MIT: relative motion using rotating axes

regime: Classical educational spacecraft simulation.
assumptions: Prescribed station rotation in LVLH with a configurable radial docking port; exact target position and velocity. Spacecraft attitude and angular rate are integrated with finite torque and propellant, rather than assumed perfect.
limitations: The station motion is prescribed; the current solver does not simulate station recoil, mechanical contact or latch dynamics.
simulation_notes: Implemented planar station spin relative to LVLH; body orientation and angular velocity are propagated rather than assumed perfect.

title: Atmospheric drag
equation: D = 0.5 rho v^2 Cd A; rho(h) = rho0 exp(-h/H)
summary: Drag opposes motion and increases with the square of speed. The atmosphere thins with altitude.
details: Our sounding rocket uses rho0=1.225 kg/m^3, H=8,500 m, Cd=0.35 and A=1 m^2. Vertical acceleration is (thrust - drag)/mass - mu/(R+h)^2. This is an educational atmosphere, not a high fidelity aerodynamic model.
regime: Classical educational spacecraft simulation.
assumptions: Exponential Earth density profile, fixed Cd and frontal area, vertical air-relative motion and no wind.
limitations: No Mach-dependent aerodynamics, lift, heating, reentry or Mars atmosphere is implemented.
simulation_notes: Used by the current backend in the restricted form described in details.

title: Numerical propagation
equation: state(t+dt) = RK4(f, state, dt); conics use analytic Kepler states
summary: The orbital simulation integrates position and velocity under gravity. The animation follows the computed samples.
details: Earth and solar two-body transfers use exact analytic Kepler conics. Launch, ball throws and docking use RK4; launch/ball scalar events are located by bisection. Docking uses sampled force/torque commands with exact propellant exhaustion splitting. Verification checks conservation, budgets, endpoint consistency and timestep convergence.
regime: Classical educational spacecraft simulation.
assumptions: Smooth force models between discrete events; units and time steps match the scenario state definitions.
limitations: The current backend uses fixed step limits, not adaptive error control, a symplectic scheme or a relativistic geodesic solver.
simulation_notes: Implemented analytic conics, RK4 finite-thrust/relative/projectile dynamics, and event location.

title: Three tiers of autonomy
equation: Physics controller -> reflex classifier -> reasoning agent
summary: Use deterministic control for frequent actions, a small classifier for discrete choices, and a reasoning model for difficult planning.
details: High-rate dynamics/control and deterministic feasibility checks sit below event/reflex routing and tool-calling reasoning. The agent retrieves knowledge and calls numerical tools; it does not replace the integrator. Executable scenarios and parameters are defined by the current MissionConfig schema and DEFAULTS. Library topics marked reference_only do not create new solver capabilities.
regime: Classical educational spacecraft simulation.
assumptions: Only scenarios supported by the current MissionConfig schema and deterministic model dispatch are executable.
limitations: Reference-only physics knowledge does not add a solver, live telemetry, hardware control or certified guidance.
simulation_notes: Current architecture: deterministic control, event/reflex routing, and bounded tool-calling reasoning. Availability of a knowledge topic is not solver support.

title: Units, constants and dimensional analysis
summary: Track units, coordinate conventions, and physical constants before applying any equation.
details: Use SI for integration: position m, velocity m/s, mass kg, time s, force N and torque N m. Angles are radians. Standard gravity g0=9.80665 m/s^2 defines specific impulse and is not local gravity. G=6.67430e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 has measurement uncertainty; c is exact. Current orbital samples report x,y in km, while docking samples use m. Black-hole assets may use Schwarzschild radii; never mix these with vehicle metres. In the current API, prefer canonical position_m and velocity_m_s SI arrays; compatibility x,y units are declared by frame.legacy_position_unit.
regime: All regimes; unit definitions precede a physical model.
assumptions: All regimes; unit definitions precede a physical model.
limitations: A numerically plausible result can still be wrong by factors of 1000 or c when units are implicit.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Inertial, body and rotating frames
equation: v_I = v_origin + R v_B + omega_I cross (R r_B)
summary: A position, velocity, or thrust direction is meaningful only with its frame and origin.
details: R maps body-frame components B into inertial-frame components I; r_B is an offset and omega_I is frame angular velocity in rad/s. A body-fixed offset gains rotational velocity. Specify origin, axis handedness, epoch and rotation convention. Docking needs station-port motion, not only station-centre motion. A render-camera frame is not an inertial dynamics frame.
regime: Classical frame transformations for differentiable rigid rotations.
assumptions: Classical frame transformations for differentiable rigid rotations.
limitations: Position rotation alone does not transform velocity between rotating frames.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Newton laws and force budgets
summary: Spacecraft acceleration follows a complete force budget, not the direction of the desired destination.
details: For fixed mass in an inertial frame, force is in N, mass in kg, and acceleration in m/s^2. Include gravity, thrust, drag and relevant disturbances. Internal forces cancel for the complete isolated assembly. Open-system rockets require momentum-flux accounting; applying F=ma to variable mass without exhaust terms is incomplete.
regime: Nonrelativistic fixed-mass systems in inertial frames.
assumptions: Nonrelativistic fixed-mass systems in inertial frames.
limitations: Use relativistic momentum in high-speed regimes and explicit flux terms for open systems.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Work, energy and power
equation: W = integral(F dot dr); K = m v^2/2; P = F dot v
summary: Energy accounting distinguishes gravity-driven acceleration from propulsion that changes the orbit.
details: W and K are in joules; P is in watts. A stationary Newtonian point-mass field has potential U=-GMm/r. Mechanical energy is conserved for an unpowered test body in that field. A burn changes kinetic energy by m*(v dot delta_v + |delta_v|^2/2) when treated as a fixed-mass impulse; a real rocket also carries energy and momentum away in exhaust.
regime: Newtonian mechanical work in a specified reference frame.
assumptions: Newtonian mechanical work in a specified reference frame.
limitations: Mechanical energy of the spacecraft alone need not be conserved during thrust or mass release.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Impulse and momentum conservation
equation: p = m v; delta_p = integral(F_external dt)
summary: Separation impulses must give equal and opposite momentum changes to the retained craft and released stage.
details: Momentum is in kg m/s and impulse in N s. Across an ideal short separation event with negligible external impulse, m1*v1+m2*v2=(m1+m2)*v_before. Specify the relative ejection speed and distribute the recoil using both masses. Zero-impulse release preserves the velocity of each point mass at that instant; it does not create an escape burn.
regime: Closed nonrelativistic system over the chosen impulse interval.
assumptions: Closed nonrelativistic system over the chosen impulse interval.
limitations: Include gas, fragments and external impulses when they carry nonnegligible momentum.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Angular momentum and orbital planes
equation: H = r cross p; dH/dt = torque_external
summary: Torque changes spin or orbital angular momentum; central gravity alone does not rotate an orbital plane.
details: Angular momentum has units kg m^2/s. For a unit-mass test body, h=r cross v in m^2/s fixes the two-body orbit plane and equals twice the swept-area rate. Off-centre thrusters and separation springs can impart torque even if their net translational force is small. Reference the angular momentum to a specified point.
regime: Newtonian mechanics with a defined origin and external torque.
assumptions: Newtonian mechanics with a defined origin and external torque.
limitations: Angular momentum about a moving origin requires the appropriate transport terms.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Centre of mass and inertia updates
summary: Jettison changes the assembly centre of mass, thrust lever arms, and inertia tensor.
details: Compute component locations in one common frame. For an extended body, integrate the mass distribution. Recompute the retained spacecraft and discarded-stage mass properties after separation or fuel consumption. A GLB origin or a visual centre-of-mass marker is not a measured physical centre of mass.
regime: Nonrelativistic material assembly with known component masses.
assumptions: Nonrelativistic material assembly with known component masses.
limitations: Uniform density inferred from visual geometry is an assumption, not engineering mass data.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Six-degree-of-freedom rigid-body dynamics
equation: m a = F; I dot(omega) + omega cross (I omega) = torque
summary: Accurate docking requires three translational and three rotational degrees of freedom.
details: The rotational equation is written in body axes for constant body-frame inertia I, with omega in rad/s and torque in N m. Propagate orientation as well as angular velocity. Use mass-flux and time-varying-inertia terms when fuel or appendages move. Station and chaser both respond to contact impulses unless one is deliberately treated as prescribed.
regime: Rigid body, nonrelativistic motion, constant inertia for the displayed Euler equation.
assumptions: Rigid body, nonrelativistic motion, constant inertia for the displayed Euler equation.
limitations: The current docking solver includes one planar attitude angle, but is not a coupled full 6-DoF contact simulation.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Quaternions and attitude kinematics
summary: Unit quaternions represent spacecraft orientation without Euler-angle gimbal lock.
details: For a scalar-first Hamilton quaternion q mapping body axes into inertial axes, omega_B is body angular velocity and tensor denotes quaternion multiplication. Normalize to control numerical drift. q and -q represent the same orientation; use the shortest rotation for error feedback and SLERP for display interpolation. State convention and multiplication order explicitly.
regime: Rigid-body orientation using the stated Hamilton and body-to-inertial convention.
assumptions: Rigid-body orientation using the stated Hamilton and body-to-inertial convention.
limitations: Library storage order and active/passive rotation conventions may differ from this equation.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Gyroscopes and rotating habitats
equation: H = I omega; a_centripetal = omega^2 R
summary: A spinning habitat provides centrifugal loading in its rotating frame and resists changes to its spin axis.
details: For spin radius R in m and omega in rad/s, the rim acceleration is omega^2 R in m/s^2. Convert rpm using omega=rpm*2*pi/60. Body inertia determines angular momentum and the torque needed to change the spin axis. Counterrotating rings can reduce net stored angular momentum but require their own dynamics and bearings.
regime: Rigid rotating structures with known spin and inertia.
assumptions: Rigid rotating structures with known spin and inertia.
limitations: A visually rotating ring does not establish structural strength, crew comfort, or bearing feasibility.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Variable-mass rocket dynamics
summary: Exhaust momentum produces thrust while the vehicle mass decreases.
details: The scalar equation assumes exhaust speed v_e is positive aft relative to the rocket and thrust acts along the positive flight direction. In vector form use the actual exhaust-relative velocity and pressure-thrust terms. Mass flow is kg/s. Fuel consumption and acceleration must be integrated together for a finite burn.
regime: Nonrelativistic directed exhaust; scalar collinear form shown.
assumptions: Nonrelativistic directed exhaust; scalar collinear form shown.
limitations: Changing vehicle mass without an exhaust momentum model does not specify thrust.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Two-body motion and Kepler conics
equation: ddot(r) = -mu r / r^3; mu = G(M + m)
summary: An isolated gravitational pair has a conic relative orbit set by its initial position and velocity.
details: r is the relative separation vector and r=|r| in m. For a negligible spacecraft mass, mu is approximately GM of the primary. Specific energy epsilon=v^2/2-mu/r determines an ellipse (negative), parabola (zero), or hyperbola (positive). This is a reference model for testing an integrator before adding perturbations.
regime: Isolated Newtonian point masses or spherical nonoverlapping bodies.
assumptions: Isolated Newtonian point masses or spherical nonoverlapping bodies.
limitations: A true lunar rendezvous needs lunar motion and gravity rather than an Earth-only endpoint marker.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Orbital elements and singular cases
equation: p = h^2/mu; r = p / (1 + e cos(f))
summary: Elements describe orbit size, shape, orientation, and phase relative to a defined central body.
details: h is specific angular-momentum magnitude; p is semilatus rectum; e is eccentricity; f is true anomaly. Classical elements are a,e,i,Omega,argument of periapsis,and anomaly at epoch. Inclination and angles need a reference plane. Circular or equatorial orbits make some classical angles undefined; use nonsingular elements or Cartesian state vectors.
regime: Osculating Keplerian elements in a chosen Newtonian frame.
assumptions: Osculating Keplerian elements in a chosen Newtonian frame.
limitations: Under perturbations the instantaneous elements evolve and do not define a permanently fixed conic.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Kepler equation and encounter timing
equation: M = E - e sin(E); n = sqrt(mu/a^3); M = n(t - t_peri)
summary: Orbit phase must be propagated in time to meet a moving target.
details: For an ellipse with a>0 and 0<=e<1, E is eccentric anomaly, M mean anomaly, and n mean motion in rad/s. Solve Kepler equation for E and convert to position. Hyperbolic motion instead uses M_h=e*sinh(H)-H and a hyperbolic anomaly H. Near-parabolic cases need numerically careful universal-variable or equivalent methods.
regime: Unperturbed elliptical two-body motion for the displayed equation.
assumptions: Unperturbed elliptical two-body motion for the displayed equation.
limitations: True anomaly is not linear in time on an eccentric orbit.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Vis-viva and specific orbital energy
summary: Local orbital speed depends on both distance from the primary and the orbit energy.
details: r and signed semi-major axis a use the same length unit; mu uses its cube per second squared. Ellipses have a>0 and hyperbolas a<0. Parabolic motion is the limit 1/a=0. At a fixed r, an impulse changes orbital energy; energy conservation is a useful coast check, but does not imply constant local speed.
regime: Newtonian unpowered two-body conic between impulses.
assumptions: Newtonian unpowered two-body conic between impulses.
limitations: Do not apply this Newtonian formula to high-speed strong-field black-hole trajectories.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Escape speed and hyperbolic excess
equation: v_escape = sqrt(2 mu/r); v_inf^2 = v^2 - 2 mu/r
summary: Escaping a central potential requires nonnegative orbital energy, not simply high altitude.
details: v_inf is asymptotic speed far from a Newtonian stationary primary. A bound orbit has negative specific energy and no real positive v_inf. Escape speed describes an ideal unpowered trajectory without atmospheric loss, later perturbations, or propulsion. A hyperbolic approach is already unbound before any periapsis burn.
regime: Stationary Newtonian point-mass field, negligible test mass.
assumptions: Stationary Newtonian point-mass field, negligible test mass.
limitations: The Schwarzschild radius is a relativistic horizon; deriving its value from Newtonian escape speed does not reproduce horizon physics.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Hyperbolic flybys and turn angle
summary: A flyby bends the velocity vector; periapsis and incoming excess speed set the turn.
details: r_p is centre-to-centre periapsis radius, not altitude; e>1. v_p=sqrt(v_inf^2+2*mu/r_p). The impact parameter is b=mu*sqrt(e^2-1)/v_inf^2. In a static Newtonian field an unpowered trajectory has equal incoming and outgoing v_inf. Compare collision radius and thermal limits before claiming a close approach is feasible.
regime: Unpowered Newtonian point-mass encounter.
assumptions: Unpowered Newtonian point-mass encounter.
limitations: Use geodesics for strong gravity; a plotted curve around a black sphere is not validation.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Gravity assists and frame-dependent energy
summary: A moving primary can exchange orbital energy with a flyby spacecraft in an external frame.
details: Compute inbound and outbound excess-velocity vectors in the primary frame, then add the primary velocity V_body in the selected inertial frame. A passive encounter preserves excess-speed magnitude in the ideal patched-conic approximation while changing direction. A stationary isolated black hole supplies no net asymptotic speed gain in its own rest frame; a powered burn or a properly modelled energy-extraction mechanism is a different process.
regime: Newtonian patched-conic encounter; reference-frame choice stated.
assumptions: Newtonian patched-conic encounter; reference-frame choice stated.
limitations: Conservation statements in one frame must not be mixed with speeds quoted in another.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Oberth effect and periapsis burns
summary: For an ideal impulse, the same prograde delta-v changes orbital energy more at higher initial speed.
details: Specific energy is J/kg and velocity is m/s in a specified inertial frame. This equation compares pre- and post-impulse test-particle states at one position. The rocket equation still determines fuel use; the effect does not create free propellant or relax thrust and thermal constraints. Near a black hole, replace Newtonian energy with conserved quantities of the chosen spacetime.
regime: Newtonian impulsive manoeuvre at fixed position.
assumptions: Newtonian impulsive manoeuvre at fixed position.
limitations: Finite-duration thrust and strong gravity can invalidate the instantaneous Newtonian calculation.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Lambert boundary-value transfers
summary: Two endpoint positions and a flight time determine candidate two-body transfer velocities.
details: Endpoint positions must share a central body, frame, length unit and epoch convention. Select prograde/retrograde and multi-revolution branches explicitly. Compare the returned velocities with the departure and target-body velocities to compute burns. Real interception needs target ephemerides, not a static endpoint at lunar radius.
regime: Newtonian two-body boundary-value problem with specified branch.
assumptions: Newtonian two-body boundary-value problem with specified branch.
limitations: A Lambert solution alone checks neither collision avoidance nor available propulsion.

title: Inclination changes and vector burns
summary: Changing the velocity direction can cost substantial fuel even when orbital speed is unchanged.
details: The displayed expression assumes equal speed v before and after a pure plane change through angle delta_i. Generally delta_v=sqrt(v1^2+v2^2-2*v1*v2*cos(angle)). Plane changes are often cheaper at lower speed near apoapsis, and may be combined with transfer burns. Orbit-plane intersection and encounter timing still matter.
regime: Instantaneous Newtonian vector velocity change.
assumptions: Instantaneous Newtonian vector velocity change.
limitations: A coplanar Hohmann budget does not include arbitrary target inclination changes.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Patched conics and encounter boundaries
summary: Piecewise two-body arcs provide a first estimate for interplanetary transfers and flybys.
details: Match position, velocity, epoch and frame at encounter boundaries. The dominant primary changes between arcs; the underlying physical acceleration changes continuously, so the patch is an approximation. Target a finite encounter geometry and use the secondary gravity for arrival capture estimates. Validate important results with multi-body propagation.
regime: Separated encounter regions with one dominant gravitational primary per arc.
assumptions: Separated encounter regions with one dominant gravitational primary per arc.
limitations: Patching can be inaccurate for weak captures and long cislunar trajectories.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Restricted three-body dynamics
summary: Two moving massive bodies can produce trajectories that no single Kepler conic can describe.
details: The displayed equation is in inertial coordinates for a negligible spacecraft mass. In the circular restricted three-body problem, the primaries orbit their barycentre circularly and rotating coordinates introduce Coriolis and centrifugal terms. A Jacobi integral exists in that autonomous rotating model, but is not a generic inertial-energy invariant.
regime: Newtonian test particle under two prescribed massive bodies.
assumptions: Newtonian test particle under two prescribed massive bodies.
limitations: The circular restricted model neglects eccentric primaries and additional perturbing bodies.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Lagrange points and station keeping
summary: Five equilibrium points exist in the circular restricted three-body rotating frame.
details: Omega_eff combines the two primary gravitational potentials with the centrifugal potential in the chosen rotating-frame convention. L1,L2,L3 are unstable. L4 and L5 are linearly stable only for an appropriate primary mass ratio. Halo and Lissajous missions orbit near these locations and require navigation and station keeping rather than remaining motionless in an inertial frame.
regime: Circular restricted three-body model with a specified effective-potential sign convention.
assumptions: Circular restricted three-body model with a specified effective-potential sign convention.
limitations: Equilibrium in rotating coordinates is not zero physical acceleration or universal stability.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Hill sphere and sphere of influence
equation: r_H approx a(1-e)(m/(3M))^(1/3); r_SOI approx a(m/M)^(2/5)
summary: These approximate scales guide encounter modelling; neither is a physical wall where gravity switches off.
details: a and e describe the secondary orbit around primary M; m is the much smaller secondary mass. The Hill expression estimates a tidal stability scale, while the Laplace sphere of influence is a different approximation used in patched conics. Track both body gravities continuously when encounter precision matters.
regime: Small secondary-to-primary mass ratio and nearly Keplerian primary-secondary motion.
assumptions: Small secondary-to-primary mass ratio and nearly Keplerian primary-secondary motion.
limitations: These radii serve different purposes and are not interchangeable capture criteria.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Perturbation force budgets
equation: a_total = a_two_body + a_J2 + a_third_body + a_drag + a_SRP + ...
summary: Select additional forces according to orbit, mission duration, and error tolerance.
details: A perturbation budget can include nonspherical gravity, the Moon and Sun, atmospheric drag, radiation pressure and manoeuvres. Evaluate the accumulated state error, not only instantaneous acceleration magnitude. Measured gravity models, Earth orientation, time scales and body ephemerides must agree in their conventions.
regime: Weak-field Newtonian orbit propagation with explicit force-model choices.
assumptions: Weak-field Newtonian orbit propagation with explicit force-model choices.
limitations: Adding an arbitrary disturbance term is not a calibrated high-fidelity model.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Oblateness and J2 precession
summary: An oblate primary produces secular node and periapsis precession.
details: Omega is the ascending-node angle; n=sqrt(mu/a^3), p=a*(1-e^2), R is the gravity-model reference radius and i inclination. J2 is dimensionless. The displayed orbit-averaged first-order rate uses a body-equatorial reference plane. Use consistent coefficients and higher-order harmonics when required by the error budget.
regime: First-order averaged J2 perturbation of a Kepler orbit.
assumptions: First-order averaged J2 perturbation of a Kepler orbit.
limitations: Not valid as a complete force model near irregular bodies or for arbitrary short-period effects.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Solar radiation pressure
equation: F_SRP approx C_R P_solar A_projected; P_solar = flux/c
summary: Sunlight transfers momentum to spacecraft surfaces and can perturb or deliberately propel an orbit.
details: flux is incident power per area in W/m^2, pressure is N/m^2, and A_projected is illuminated area normal to the rays. For ideal normal incidence C_R ranges from 1 for absorption to 2 for specular reflection; real geometry and optical properties determine the vector force. Include eclipse and inverse-square solar flux changes.
regime: Photon momentum transfer with a stated surface-optics model.
assumptions: Photon momentum transfer with a stated surface-optics model.
limitations: A single scalar C_R does not reproduce all reflection directions or complex shadowing.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: N-body gravitational propagation
summary: Sum consistent gravitational interactions instead of abruptly switching primaries.
details: Use one inertial or correctly transformed reference system. For test-particle propagation, integrate the spacecraft against body states from ephemerides; for a self-consistent closed N-body system, integrate all interacting masses. Avoid singular encounters and double counting the central term. Barycentric and primary-relative formulations require different indirect terms.
regime: Newtonian point masses or appropriately expanded extended-body gravity.
assumptions: Newtonian point masses or appropriately expanded extended-body gravity.
limitations: This equation excludes relativity and does not by itself specify body ephemerides.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Thrust, specific impulse and mass flow
equation: F = dot(m)_exhaust v_e + (p_e-p_ambient) A_e; Isp = F/(dot(m)_exhaust g0)
summary: Thrust sets acceleration while specific impulse measures propellant efficiency.
details: Exhaust mass flow is positive in kg/s, v_e in m/s, pressure in Pa, and nozzle exit area A_e in m^2. Effective exhaust speed is Isp*g0; pressure thrust is included in that effective value. Isp in seconds is not thrust or burn duration. Propagation needs engine limits, throttle, pointing and available propellant as well as Isp.
regime: Continuum nonrelativistic rocket exhaust with specified nozzle and environment.
assumptions: Continuum nonrelativistic rocket exhaust with specified nozzle and environment.
limitations: Constant Isp and thrust are approximations; performance varies with engine and ambient pressure.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Multistage rockets and discarded dry mass
summary: Discarding expended structure improves later burn mass ratios without an arbitrary free velocity increase.
details: For each stage, both mass-ratio endpoints bracket the burn before any following dry-stage discard; remaining upper stages and payload are included. Then subtract the released dry mass before calculating the next burn. At a zero-impulse release, position and translational velocity remain continuous for point masses. Subsequent acceleration and available delta-v change because the retained mass is lower.
regime: Sequential ideal nonrelativistic burns with explicit mass bookkeeping.
assumptions: Sequential ideal nonrelativistic burns with explicit mass bookkeeping.
limitations: Do not count a dry-mass drop as expelled high-speed propellant in the rocket equation.
simulation_notes: Knowledge reference only; this topic does not enable an additional mission solver.

title: Stage separation, recoil and tip-off
equation: delta_v1 = J/m1; delta_v2 = -J/m2; delta_H = r_lever cross J
summary: A release mechanism distributes an impulse and can change both bodies translation and spin.
